pieces.title: Resolution 1 — Why a separate language, and how it was wired to the page
pieces.content:
You asked four things. This takes them in order, all the way down.

Part 0 — What actually happened when you clicked something in 1994

Before the objection can be answered, the cost you are trying to avoid has to be real rather than asserted. Here is the full physical sequence when a user submitted a form.

The browser opens a TCP connection to the server. TCP requires a three-way handshake — SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK — before a single byte of your data moves. That is one full round trip spent agreeing to talk.

Then the browser sends the request. A form submission is encoded as application/x-www-form-urlencoded, which is where the familiar shape comes from:

POST /cgi-bin/register.pl HTTP/1.0
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
Content-Length: 52

name=Devansh&email=devansh%40example&city=Noida

The server passes this to a CGI program — Common Gateway Interface, from NCSA httpd in 1993. The web server spawns an entirely new operating-system process, hands it the form data, waits for it to print a complete HTML page to standard output, and sends that back. A fresh process per submission.

That program checks the email, finds no @, and writes out a whole new page saying so. The connection closes — HTTP/1.0 had no persistent connections by default — so the next request starts from the TCP handshake again.

Now the numbers. On a 28.8 kbit/s modem, round-trip latency was typically 150–400 ms and throughput about 3.5 kilobytes per second. So: one round trip for the handshake, another to send the request, a process spawn and script run on the server, and then a modest 8 KB page taking over two seconds to transfer. Call it two and a half to four seconds, during which the browser shows a blank or half-drawn page and the user can do nothing.

Your account of the multi-error case is exactly right, including the part most people miss — the re-typing. Since the server returned a new page, whatever the user had typed was gone unless the CGI author had gone to the trouble of writing every value back into the HTML as VALUE="..." attributes. Many did not. So a wrong email address could cost you the whole form.

Four errors found one at a time, at three seconds each, with re-typing in between, is a minute of a person's life to discover a missing @ — a check taking a computer roughly a microsecond, on a machine already on their desk, already holding the data.

That gap — microseconds of work, seconds of waiting, on data already local — is the entire reason this node exists.

Part 1 — Your objection, taken seriously

First, what is true. HTML 2.0 — RFC 1866, November 1995 — standardised the form controls, and they predate JavaScript; forms had been in Mosaic since 1993. So <input>, <select>, <textarea>, checkboxes, radio buttons and submit buttons were all there before any script existed.

Two corrections. <dialog> is HTML5, standardised around 2014 — not part of the 1995 picture. And lists are not interactivity; they are structure.

Now the distinction that resolves the objection: HTML gives you controls. It does not give you behaviour.

A checkbox exists; a user ticks it. Exactly two things can follow, both decided by the browser: it redraws the box with a tick, and on submission that value is included in what goes to the server. There is no third. You cannot express "when this is ticked, reveal those fields," or "if this box lacks an @, say so." Each needs a condition — if this, then that — and HTML has no grammar for conditions.

HTML is declarative: it declares what things are. <input type="text"> says "a text box exists here." There is no place in that sentence to attach "and when something happens, do this."

The sharpest way to see it: in 1995 the only thing a page could do in response to user input was submit a form. The entire interactive vocabulary of the web was fill in fields, press submit, wait, receive a new page. Every interaction, however trivial, was a page navigation.

Part 2 — Why not just add conditions to HTML? They did, twice, and neither worked

Attempt one: more attributes — which actually happened

About twenty years later, HTML5 added exactly what you are describing:

<input type="email" required>
<input type="text" pattern="[0-9]{6}" title="Six digits">
<input type="number" min="1" max="10">

Get it wrong and the browser blocks submission and shows a message, with no JavaScript. Your instinct was sound enough that the standards process eventually agreed with it.

And yet almost every real form still validates in JavaScript. Watch what happens as requirements leave the pre-built list: required only if another box is ticked; two fields that must match; a username checked against the server as you type; the error shown beside the field in your own styling and language; a date at least eighteen years ago; three values whose total must not exceed a fourth.

None are expressible as attributes. And the fix shows why the approach cannot work. You would need required-if, then must-match, then min-age, then sum-max — a new attribute for every requirement anyone has ever had. Each must be proposed to a standards body, agreed by every vendor, implemented separately, and then waited out until enough users have a browser that supports it. In the 1990s that wait was measured in years, because browsers shipped on CDs.

So the vocabulary grows without bound and is always behind what people need. The alternative is one thing that can express any behaviour — variables, conditions, the ability to receive new instructions without shipping a new browser. That is what a programming language is.

Notice the shift in power. With attributes, the browser vendor decides what is possible and you wait. With a language, you decide, and ship it today, in the same file.

Attempt two: Java applets — the alternative that shipped and lost

In 1995 the obvious answer to "the web needs programs" was not a new language. It was Java, announced by Sun in May 1995 with enormous force. Netscape Navigator 2.0 shipped with a Java virtual machine built in. Java applets — real compiled programs running inside the page — were the future everyone expected.

They failed for reasons that map precisely onto your question.

They started slowly. The JVM had to initialise before anything ran; users watched a grey rectangle for several seconds, on a connection already costing seconds per page.

They needed a compile step. You wrote .java, compiled to .class bytecode, uploaded it. You could not open the page source and adjust something. The audience — writers, designers, academics — was locked out.

And decisively: they could not touch the page. An applet was a rectangle. The browser handed it a box of pixels and it drew inside. It could not read your form's text box, could not change the heading, could not hide a paragraph. It was a separate program parked on the page, not part of it.

That is exactly what you were reaching for when you asked how a script could control parts of the screen. Applets could not, and that is why they lost. What was needed was something that started instantly, needed no compilation, was editable by non-programmers, and could reach into the page the browser had already built. Eich's brief was explicitly a companion to Java: Java for serious components, a small scripting language for the page. The small one turned out to be the one people needed.

There was a third attempt. Microsoft shipped VBScript alongside its JavaScript clone (JScript) in Internet Explorer 3.0, August 1996. It only ever worked in Internet Explorer, so writing it meant abandoning half your audience. It died on the web and survived only inside corporate intranets that mandated IE.

Part 3 — How the script was joined to the page

Three mechanisms, all in Netscape Navigator 2.0 — beta as LiveScript in September 1995, renamed JavaScript on 4 December 1995, released March 1996.

Mechanism 1: the code lived inside the page

You pictured two files. In 1995 it was usually one:

<HTML>
<HEAD>
<SCRIPT LANGUAGE="JavaScript">
<!--
function checkEmail() {
  var v = document.reg.email.value;
  if (v.indexOf("@") == -1) {
    alert("Please enter a valid email address.");
    return false;
  }
  return true;
}
// -->
</SCRIPT>
</HEAD>
<BODY>
<FORM NAME="reg" ACTION="/cgi-bin/register.pl" METHOD="POST"
      onSubmit="return checkEmail()">
  <INPUT TYPE="text" NAME="email">
  <INPUT TYPE="submit" VALUE="Send">
</FORM>
</BODY>
</HTML>

Period-accurate, down to the uppercase tags. That is your form-validation example, working, in 1996.

Now the <!-- and // -->. That is an HTML comment wrapping the code. Browsers that had never heard of <script> — in 1996, most of them — follow a rule that says ignore tags you do not recognise, but render their contents. Without the comment, those users saw the source code printed on the page as text. The comment made old browsers skip it, while browsers that understood <script> knew to ignore the markers. The // is needed because --> is not valid JavaScript — the comment has to be hidden from the script engine as well as shown to the parser. Two languages negotiating in three characters.

Note what that trick is: a workaround so a new capability does not break the experience for software that predates it. Hold that thought for Part 5.

Mechanism 2: attributes whose value is code

Here is the actual bridge:

<FORM NAME="reg" onSubmit="return checkEmail()">

onSubmit sits in the markup like NAME or TYPE. But its value is neither text nor a number — it is JavaScript source. The browser stores that string and, when the form is submitted, executes it.

Mechanically, the browser takes the attribute's string and effectively wraps it in a function:

function (event) { return checkEmail(); }

That is not a metaphor — it is why return false works there but would be a syntax error at the top level of a script. The attribute's contents are a function body.

Netscape 2.0 shipped a small family: onClick, onSubmit, onChange, onFocus, onBlur, onMouseOver, onLoad. Markup declares structure; a handful of attributes hand specific moments to the script.

Two consequences that resurface later in the chain. The return value is meaningful — onSubmit inspects it, and false cancels the submission. That is what stops the round trip from Part 0; the browser never opens a socket. And this inside the handler is the element: in onClick="this.value='clicked'", this is the button. That is the origin of the DOM half of Node 5's this rules — the browser calls your handler with the element bound as the receiver.

Mechanism 3: the page as objects the script can reach

The deepest part, and the direct answer: the script does not control the screen. It cannot draw. It has no access to pixels.

What happens is that the browser, while parsing the HTML, builds objects in memory representing what it found. A <form> becomes a form object; an <input> becomes an object with a value property. The script reads and writes those objects, and the browser redraws from them.

document.reg.email.value

means: on document, find the form named reg; on it, the input named email; read its value. Three property lookups. No pixels anywhere.

In 1995 that object model was crude and fixed — retroactively called DOM Level 0. You got a handful of collections: document.forms, document.images, document.links, document.anchors, document.title, window.location.

There was no getElementById — that came with the W3C's DOM Level 1 in October 1998. No creating elements, no changing arbitrary text, no restructuring. You could read and write form values, swap document.images[0].src (how every 1990s rollover worked), and write text into the page while it was still loading.

The asymmetry is worth stating plainly, because it explains the shape of the whole first decade: the script could read and modify things that already existed, but could not create structure. Anything you wanted to change had to be in the HTML already, sitting hidden. That is why 1990s pages are full of hidden elements toggled into view, and why "dynamic HTML" felt like a trick rather than a capability until DOM Level 1 arrived.

Part 4 — Why a script blocked the page from rendering

The browser's pipeline runs roughly:

bytes → tokenizer → parser → object tree (DOM) → layout → paint

The tokenizer chews the HTML into tokens; the parser assembles them into the object tree; layout computes where everything sits; paint draws it. This is a stream — the browser starts drawing before the file has finished arriving, which is why 1990s pages appeared progressively, top-down.

Now the parser reaches <script>. It must decide: keep parsing while the script runs, or stop? It has no choice but to stop, because of this:

<SCRIPT LANGUAGE="JavaScript">
document.write("<P>Hello, it is " + new Date() + "</P>");
</SCRIPT>

document.write does not modify the finished page. It injects raw text into the tokenizer's input stream at the exact position the parser has reached. The parser then tokenizes what the script just wrote as though it had been in the file all along.

So the parser cannot advance past a <script> before running it — the script may be about to hand it more source. Worse, the script can write an unbalanced fragment such as document.write("<TABLE><TR><TD>"), leaving the parser mid-element with the rest of the file completing the structure. Parsing ahead speculatively is therefore not merely wasteful but incorrect.

That is the architectural fact you were reaching for. It is not that anyone feared scripts freezing pages; it is that document.write's design made blocking mandatory. And because parsing blocks, the object tree stops growing, so layout stops, so paint stops. A slow script is a page that has stopped appearing.

This is not history. Put a slow <script src="…"> in the <head> today and you get a white screen until it loads — still the most common cause of slow-feeling sites. The escapes came later, and both are promises not to use document.write: defer (HTML 4.0, December 1997) keeps parsing and runs the script after the document is parsed, in order; async (HTML5) keeps parsing and runs it whenever it arrives. Both exist solely because the default had to be blocking.

And now the connection forward. The chain runs: document.write exists → the parser must block on scripts → a slow script freezes the page → "never block the page" becomes a hard constraint on the language. The single thread, the callbacks, the event loop you meet at Node 9 — the entire second half of the language — descends from a rule established here in 1995, by a function almost nobody uses any more.

Part 5 — Two places where I was loose, and you caught one

In the landscape I listed four constraints as one family. Three genuinely belong together — start instantly, do not touch the machine, do not freeze the page — because all three follow from this code arrived from a stranger and runs on your computer.

"Never break old pages" is not in that family. It has nothing to do with trust. It comes from a different property of the web: publish once, abandon forever.

Installed software has an update path: the vendor ships version 2, you update. The web has none. A page published in 1997 is still served, byte for byte, by a machine nobody has logged into in fifteen years, written by someone unreachable. If a browser changes how it interprets something, that page breaks permanently, with no possible remedy — and a browser that breaks pages loses users to one that does not. The pressure is commercial as much as technical.

That is why the language can only add, never change, and why you have three ways to declare a variable — which is what your Q4 and Q5 push on, and which deserves its own piece.

The second correction — your sandbox guess

Your reasoning is sound but the history runs the other way. Tabs did not exist in 1995. Tabbed browsing arrived with Opera and the Mozilla suite around 2000–2003. And process isolation — each tab as a separate operating-system process, so one crashing or being compromised cannot reach another — came with Google Chrome in 2008, thirteen years later. Site isolation is later still, hardened after the Spectre disclosures in 2018.

So the 1995 "sandbox" was far weaker than you pictured. It was not enforced by the operating system. It was enforced by absence: the language simply had no filesystem API, no process API, no network API beyond fetching a URL. You could not open a file because there was no function that opened files. Security by not providing the capability.

The one genuine security boundary from that era is the same-origin policy, introduced in Netscape 2.0 in 1995, and it is the real ancestor of what you were describing: a script from bank.com cannot read the contents of a page from mail.com, even if both are open. Without it, any page you visited could read your webmail. That policy is why CORS exists.

So your instinct that isolation matters was right; the mechanism you attributed it to arrived thirteen years later.

Part 6 — What using it was actually like

The code was plain text in the page, delivered as-is. Anyone could choose View → Source and read the complete working source of every script on any site. No compilation, no minification, no build step. If you liked what a page did, you read exactly how, and pasted it into your file.

That is how essentially everyone learned JavaScript for its first decade — not from books, from view-source. Enormous numbers of pages ran near-identical validation snippets propagated by copy-paste, mutating slightly at each hop. The same three or four scripts, subtly corrupted, ran on thousands of sites.

It also compounds the ten days from Node 0: whatever shipped was immediately and permanently visible to everyone, and being copied within days. There was no quiet window in which to fix it.

And then it got standardised anyway. Microsoft reverse-engineered the language for Internet Explorer 3.0 in August 1996, calling it JScript to avoid Sun's trademark. Two independent implementations of an undocumented language immediately began to diverge, and pages started working in one browser and not the other. Netscape submitted the language to Ecma International in November 1996, and ECMA-262 edition 1 was published in June 1997.

Which means the ten-day design was frozen into an international standard within eighteen months, at a moment when nobody could yet see which parts were mistakes. That is the mechanism by which a rushed prototype became permanent.

What this resolves

Your follow-upWhat answers it
Q1 — why not extend HTML?Parts 1–2: HTML gives controls, not behaviour. They did add validation attributes twenty years later and it still is not enough. Applets were the serious alternative and lost.
Q1 — how were script and page connected?Part 3: <script> inside the page, event attributes whose value is a function body, and an object tree the script reads and writes
Q1 — what did it actually look like?Parts 3 and 6: period code, the comment-wrapping trick, view-source culture
Q1 — why was the round trip so bad?Part 0: TCP handshake, CGI process spawn, HTTP/1.0 without keep-alive, ~3 s per attempt, and re-typing the form each time
Q7 — how could a script affect rendering?Part 4: document.write injects into the tokenizer stream, so blocking is mandatory rather than cautious
Q7 — sandboxing and tab isolationPart 5: right instinct, wrong mechanism — tabs are ~2001, process isolation is Chrome 2008. The 1995 boundary was the same-origin policy and the absence of dangerous APIs.
Q7 — how does "never break old pages" relate to untrusted code?Part 5: it does not. My framing conflated two different pressures.

Seven distinct doubts, one explanation.
